unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: In this unit you learn to talk about emotions (how we feel), behaviour (how we act) and identity (who we are and where our family comes from). You meet children who feel nervous, curious, proud and shy, and who learn to be gentle, polite and generous towards others. You practise saying how you feel, giving kind advice, and describing what makes your own family special. By the end you will be ready for the unit story, “The Day of the Play,” in which Amal finds her courage on stage.
unit.learningPath:
Start with the Vocabulary file. Learn a few words each day and tick your Word Wall.
Work through the seven mini-lessons in the Grammar file, one at a time — never all at once!
Read the Story file, “The Day of the Play,” and answer the questions.
Work through the four skills below: Reading & Listening → Speaking → Writing → Activities.
Finish with the Self-Assessment to see what you have learned, and get ready for Unit 8.

visual.alt: Children expressing emotions, behaviour and identity respectfully

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Feeling worried or a little afraid about something that might happen.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Amal felt nervous before her big spelling test at school.
practiceSentences: My knees felt nervous as I waited behind the curtain.
Sami's hands shook because he was nervous about the recital.
Do new places make you feel nervous sometimes?
"Everyone gets nervous before a race," said the coach kindly.
I felt nervous when the dentist called my name.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: n - e - r - v - o - u - s
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult beside you, tell the tutor about one moment that makes you nervous, then ask for two calming ideas.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Feeling very worried, with lots of worried thoughts that will not go away.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: She was anxious about walking home in the dark.
practiceSentences: Waiting for the exam results made me feel very anxious.
Nora felt anxious as the storm clouds gathered overhead.
Why were you anxious about the spelling test?
"When I feel anxious, I take deep breaths," said Maya.
I was anxious about the results until Father hugged me.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: a - n - x - i - o - u - s
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask the tutor, while your helper listens, to explain how anxious is stronger than nervous, then test yourself with two sentences.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Feeling extremely frightened by something that scares you very badly indeed.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: I was terrified when I saw the huge spider.
practiceSentences: My cousin was terrified of the thunder last night.
The kitten was terrified of the roaring vacuum cleaner.
What made you so terrified during the film?
"I am terrified of heights," admitted Karim the window cleaner.
I felt terrified when the lights went out suddenly.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: t - e - r - r - i - f - i - e - d
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: With your helper nearby, ask the tutor to put scared, frightened and terrified in order of strength, and say why.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Not sure that something is true or that it will really happen.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: He felt doubtful about winning the game.
practiceSentences: Leo looked doubtful about winning the spelling contest.
Maya looked doubtful when Theo said he saw a falcon.
Why are you doubtful that the seeds will grow?
"The weather looks doubtful for our picnic," said Mother.
I was doubtful about the new recipe, but it tasted great.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: d - o - u - b - t - f - u - l
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Read the tutor two sentences, one certain and one doubtful, with an adult listening, and ask it to spot the doubtful one.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Really wanting to know or learn something new about the world.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The curious cat looked inside the open box.
practiceSentences: A curious puppy sniffed every corner of the garden.
The curious child asked questions about everything in the museum.
Are you curious about what lives inside the coral reef?
"Stay curious and keep asking questions," said Teacher Yasmin.
I was curious about the strange noise in the attic.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: c - u - r - i - o - u - s
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Sit with an adult and ask the tutor three curious questions about how the dishwasher in your kitchen works.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Feeling happy about something you did or about who you are.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: I am proud of my drawing because I worked hard on it.
practiceSentences: Mum looked proud when I read my poem aloud.
Adam felt proud when he finished the whole race.
Are you proud of the garden you planted?
"We are proud of your honesty," said the head teacher.
I felt proud when my little sister read her first book.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: p - r - o - u - d
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Tell the tutor, with your helper present, about one thing you are proud of, and ask it to turn your words into one strong sentence.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Kind and soft in the way you act; not rough or loud.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: She gave the puppy a gentle hug.
practiceSentences: Please use gentle hands when you hold the rabbit.
Theo was gentle when he held the baby chick.
Can you be gentle while brushing the cat?

My grandmother's gentle hands wrapped my scraped knee carefully.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: g - e - n - t - l - e
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask the tutor, while an adult listens, for three ways to say something in a gentle voice instead of a rough one.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Showing good manners and treating other people kindly with your words.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: It is polite to say please and thank you.
practiceSentences: A polite hello can make a new pupil feel welcome.
The polite boy held the door open for his teacher.
What is the polite way to ask for help?
"Being polite costs nothing at all," Grandfather always says.

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: p - o - l - i - t - e
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult beside you, act out asking for help twice, and ask the tutor which version sounded more polite.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Happy to share what you have, or to give things to others.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The generous boy gave his snack to a friend.
practiceSentences: It was generous of Nora to lend me her coat.
The generous baker gave extra bread to the poor family.
Who was generous enough to share their umbrella today?

My generous friend gave me half of her sandwich.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: g - e - n - e - r - o - u - s
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask the tutor, with your helper nearby, to describe one generous action you could do at school this week.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Only caring about yourself and not about how other people feel.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: It was selfish to take all the biscuits and share none.
practiceSentences: Keeping the whole box of crayons would be selfish.
The selfish king in the story kept all the water.
Is it selfish to want the swing all break time?
"Sharing stops us from being selfish," said Mother.
I felt selfish after hiding the coloured pencils, so I apologised.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: s - e - l - f - i - s - h
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult present, ask the tutor to name the opposite of selfish and to explain the difference in one short sentence.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Not joking or silly; important and needing your full attention.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: She had a serious look on her face.
practiceSentences: The referee gave a serious warning to both teams.
The doctor wore a serious face while reading the chart.
Why did the meeting sound so serious today?

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: s - e - r - i - o - u - s
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask the tutor, while your helper listens, to read one serious line and one silly line so you can hear the difference.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Funny in a clever way, so that people around you laugh.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The teacher told a humorous story, and everyone laughed.
practiceSentences: Our class play had a humorous lion who kept roaring.
Grandfather told a humorous tale about a runaway goat.

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: h - u - m - o - r - o - u - s
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Tell the tutor a humorous two-line joke with an adult listening, then ask which word made it funny.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Very strong, powerful or angry, in a way that can frighten.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The fierce wind blew the leaves off the trees.
practiceSentences: The lion in our play gave one fierce roar.
A fierce storm rattled the windows all night long.
How does a lion's fierce roar warn other animals?

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: f - i - e - r - c - e
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult beside you, ask the tutor which nouns pair well with fierce, such as storm, roar and debate.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Very bad or cruel, wanting to cause harm to other people.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The story had an evil villain who wanted to hurt people.
practiceSentences: An evil dragon guarded the treasure in the old tale.
The evil wizard in the tale locked away the sunshine.
Why do stories often end with the evil character losing?

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: e - v - i - l
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask the tutor, with your helper present, why story writers give us evil characters, and how those characters usually end.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Quiet and a little afraid to talk to people you do not know.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The shy girl hid behind her mother.
practiceSentences: The shy new girl stood alone beside the wall.
The shy new student ate lunch alone at first.
Were you shy on your first day of school?
"Do not be shy; come join our game," said Theo.
I was too shy to sing, so I hummed quietly instead.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: s - h - y
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult nearby, ask the tutor for three friendly sentences you could say to somebody who feels shy.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Belonging to a group who share the same culture, language or history.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: In our class we celebrate many ethnic traditions.
practiceSentences: Our school fair celebrates the ethnic traditions of every family.
The festival displayed ethnic dishes from ten different countries.
Which ethnic dress will you wear for the celebration?

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: e - t - h - n - i - c
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Sit with an adult and tell the tutor about one family tradition, then ask it to use the word ethnic in its reply.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To make somebody or something move closer to you.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The bright flowers attract many bees.
practiceSentences: Warm lights attract moths to the window at night.
Bright feeders attract many birds to the school garden.

My shiny marbles attract attention at every break time.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: a - t - t - r - a - c - t
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask the tutor, while your helper listens, to give two science examples and two everyday examples of things that attract.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Likely to be dangerous, or to end with a bad result.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Riding a bike without a helmet is risky.
practiceSentences: Running across the busy road would be very risky.
Crossing the stream on wet stones is very risky.

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: r - i - s - k - y
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult present, list two risky actions and two safe ones for the tutor, and ask it to check your reasons.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Happening often, again and again over a short time.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: We take frequent breaks during our lessons.
practiceSentences: Our teacher gives frequent reminders about kind words.

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: f - r - e - q - u - e - n - t
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask the tutor, with an adult beside you, to change frequent into frequently and to build one sentence with each form.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A machine that washes dirty plates, cups and spoons for you.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: We put the dirty plates in the dishwasher after dinner.
practiceSentences: Our kitchen dishwasher rumbles softly after every family meal.

dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: d - i - s - h - w - a - s - h - e - r
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: With your helper nearby, name five machines in your home for the tutor and ask which job the dishwasher does best.

rubrics.level1: Speaks very quietly, and the listener misses most words.
rubrics.level2: Some words are clear, but the pace changes and endings drop away.
rubrics.level3: Speaks clearly at a steady pace, and the listener follows easily.
rubrics.level4: Speaks clearly and confidently, adjusting volume and pace for the listener.

rubrics.level1: Uses one or two unit words, sometimes with the wrong meaning.
rubrics.level2: Uses three or four unit words correctly, with some repetition.
rubrics.level3: Uses five or more unit words accurately across the task.
rubrics.level4: Chooses precise feelings and behaviour words, and explains shades of meaning.

rubrics.level1: Answers in single words or unfinished phrases.
rubrics.level2: Uses complete sentences, though tenses slip in longer turns.
rubrics.level3: Uses complete sentences with accurate present perfect and past simple forms.
rubrics.level4: Varies sentence openers and keeps every verb form accurate.

rubrics.level1: Waits to be asked and rarely replies to the other speaker.
rubrics.level2: Answers questions, but does not ask any.
rubrics.level3: Asks and answers questions, and takes turns politely.
rubrics.level4: Builds on what the partner said and extends the talk with new questions.

rubrics.level1: One idea only, with no supporting detail.
rubrics.level2: Two ideas, with detail on one of them.
rubrics.level3: Several linked ideas, each with a supporting detail.
rubrics.level4: Well-chosen ideas with vivid detail that shows the writer's feelings.

rubrics.level1: Sentences appear in no clear order.
rubrics.level2: The order mostly works, but the ending stops suddenly.
rubrics.level3: A clear beginning, middle and ending, joined by connectives.
rubrics.level4: Paragraphs or sections are shaped for the reader, with strong links between them.

rubrics.level1: Everyday words only, with several repeated verbs.
rubrics.level2: Some unit vocabulary, though word choice is often general.
rubrics.level3: Accurate unit vocabulary and controlled verb tenses throughout.
rubrics.level4: Precise vocabulary and varied sentence structures that strengthen the message.

rubrics.level1: Capital letters and full stops are missing in most sentences.
rubrics.level2: Basic punctuation is present, but unit words are often misspelled.
rubrics.level3: Sentence punctuation is accurate and unit words are spelled correctly.
rubrics.level4: Punctuation, including speech marks and commas, is accurate and purposeful.

readings.title: The Day Before the Test
readings.setting: School, home and community settings familiar to learners
readings.passageScript:
Amal sat quietly at the kitchen table, staring at her spelling list. Tomorrow was her big spelling test, and she felt nervous every time she looked at the long words.
Her thoughts were anxious ones: “What if I forget the words? What if my mind goes blank in front of the whole class?”
Her older brother Adam came in and saw her worried face. He was always gentle with her, even when he was busy with his own homework.
“Don’t be so hard on yourself,” he said kindly, pulling out the chair beside her. “You have studied every day this week. I have felt nervous before a test too, and it was fine in the end.”
“Really?” Amal asked, looking doubtful. “You always seem so calm.”
“Everybody feels nervous sometimes,” Adam said. “The trick is not to let the worry win.”
Amal was still doubtful, but she felt a little braver. She read through her list one more time, sounding out each tricky word.
After dinner, Mum brought her a cup of warm milk and sat beside her on the sofa. “Be polite to your worry,” Mum said with a smile, “listen to it calmly, and then tell it to go to sleep.”
Amal laughed, and the tight feeling in her chest loosened a little.
The next morning, Amal walked into the classroom with her list still fresh in her mind. When the test was over, she felt proud, because she had remembered every single word.

readings.title: Where My Family Comes From
readings.setting: School, home and community settings familiar to learners
readings.passageScript:
My name is Nora, and I am proud of who I am.
My family comes from a small town beside the river, where the water moves slowly past old stone bridges. We speak two languages at home, and only English at school, so my head is always busy switching between them.
On special days my grandmother sits by the window and tells stories about her childhood in that same small town. She also bakes sweet honey cakes for our guests, filling the whole house with a warm smell of cinnamon.
“A guest is a gift,” my grandmother always says, and she means it. Even when visitors arrive without any warning, she never lets anyone leave hungry.
My friends come from many ethnic groups. Some families are from the city, some from farming villages, and some from other countries far across the sea. Maya’s family speaks three languages, and Sami’s grandparents grow olives on a hillside.
At school we sometimes bring food from home to share at lunchtime, and everybody is curious to try something new.
We are all different, and I think that is wonderful. Being kind and generous to each other is the most important thing, whatever language you speak at home or wherever your family comes from.

readings.title: Getting Ready for the Play
readings.setting: School, home and community settings familiar to learners
readings.passageScript:
Teacher Yasmin: “Good morning, class. Tomorrow is our school play, and I know some of you feel nervous. That is completely normal! Even actors on the biggest stages feel nervous before the curtain goes up.
Remember three things. First, you have practised hard every single day this week, so you are ready. You know your lines, your songs, and your places on the stage.
Second, be gentle and polite to each other backstage. It will be busy back there, with costumes, masks and props everywhere. Don’t be selfish with the costumes — share the mirror, and help each other with the buttons you cannot reach.
Third, if you make a small mistake, just smile and keep going. Nobody in the audience will notice a tiny slip if you stay calm.”
Sami: “What if I forget my lines completely?”
Teacher Yasmin: “Then look at a friend on stage. We have all practised together, and we will help each other.
I am so proud of every one of you, and I know your families will be proud too. Now, let’s do one more run-through before home time!”

readings.title: A Chat About Feelings
readings.setting: School, home and community settings familiar to learners
readings.passageScript:
Maya: “How do you feel today, Nora?”
Nora: “I feel curious! We are visiting a cultural fair tomorrow. Have you ever been to one?”
Maya: “Yes, I have. I went last year, and I felt so proud to show my family’s food. Why are you curious?”
Nora: “Because I have never tried food from so many different places before! What did your family bring to the fair?”
Maya: “We brought a big tray of rice and spiced chicken. My little brother helped carry the plates, even though he felt shy at first.”
Nora: “That sounds delicious. Were you nervous standing behind the table?”
Maya: “A little, at the start. But everyone was so polite, and lots of people asked kind questions about our food. By the end I wasn’t nervous at all.”
Nora: “I hope I feel that brave tomorrow. Maybe I will try five new foods!”
Maya: “You should! And don’t be shy about asking people questions — most families are proud to talk about where their food comes from.”
Nora: “Thanks, Maya. Now I am even more curious about tomorrow!”

readings.title: The Day of the Play
readings.setting: School, home and community settings familiar to learners
readings.passageScript:
Amal stood behind the school curtain, holding her costume. She looked out at the rows of chairs, all filled with parents. Her hands shook a little.
“I’m so nervous,” she whispered.
“You’ll be great,” said her friend Sami. “You’ve practised every single line.”
Amal tried to smile. This was the first time she had ever been in a school play. She had the main part, the kind queen who helps people in need. Teacher Yasmin had told her, “Amal, you should be proud. You’ve worked so hard.”
Still, Amal felt anxious. What if she forgot her words? What if the lights were too bright?
“You mustn’t be so hard on yourself,” said Sami. “Just be gentle and speak politely, like the queen in the story.”
Amal nodded. “Thanks. I’ll try.”
Earlier that week the whole class had worked hard on the costumes. Sami wore a lion mask. Amal’s little brother, Idris, came to watch with their parents.
At home the night before, Idris had told her, “Don’t be shy, Amal. You always help me with my homework. You can talk in front of people.”
Amal had laughed. “Talking to you is much easier!”
“But you’ve done harder things,” Idris said. “Remember the fierce rainstorm? You helped Mum carry the water buckets in the wind. That was risky!”
She smiled now as she remembered that day.
The lights in the hall came on. The show began.
First, the lion walked onto the stage. Sami frequently made the crowd laugh with his funny, humorous roars. The queen had to stop him.
Amal stepped out. Her voice was quiet at first, but it grew stronger and stronger.
“You must not act wild,” she told the lion, in a serious voice. “We must be polite and kind.”
The audience clapped.
As the play went on, Amal forgot to feel anxious. She looked at the people in front of her. Mothers wore colourful ethnic dresses, and children had come from many different backgrounds. Fathers watched with proud smiles. She felt calm.
At the end, the queen gives her crown to a poor child. Amal bent down and said softly, “This crown is not just for me. A good leader must be generous.”
The whole crowd stood up and cheered.
Backstage, Teacher Yasmin clapped. “Amal, you were amazing!”
Amal grinned. “I don’t feel shy any more.”
After the play the students helped tidy up. Amal and Sami went to wash the paint brushes in the art-room sink. “Let’s put these in the dishwasher,” said Sami, pointing at the sink.
“You know that’s not a real dishwasher!” Amal said, laughing.
Outside, a new student stood alone near the wall. She looked terrified. Amal walked over and said, “Hi, I’m Amal. Did you like the play?”
The girl nodded but did not speak.
“She seems doubtful,” whispered Sami.
“She’s probably just curious, or maybe nervous,” Amal said. “Let’s be kind. It would be selfish to leave her on her own.”
They brought her a chair and a cool drink.
“You were very gentle on the stage,” the girl said at last.
“Thank you!” Amal smiled. “You’re welcome to play with us next time.”
That night Amal wrote in her notebook:
“Today I was scared, but I found my courage. I used a gentle voice and I spoke politely. I have felt anxious before, but now I know that the feeling passes. I have also been shy, but helping someone made me feel better. I have learned that being kind is much better than being selfish. I am not just proud of the play; I am proud of how I behaved.”
Her mother walked in. “You’re still awake?”
“I’m writing about my day,” Amal said.
“You should be proud,” her mother said gently. “You’ve grown in so many ways.”
Amal closed her notebook and turned off the light. She smiled and whispered, “I’m ready for tomorrow.”

comprehension.question: Why did Amal feel nervous while she sat at the kitchen table?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She felt nervous because her big spelling test was the very next day.
comprehension.explanation: The text names the spelling test and links it directly to the word nervous.

comprehension.question: Where does Nora say her family comes from?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Nora's family comes from a small town beside the river.
comprehension.explanation: The second line of the recount gives the location directly.

comprehension.question: What three things does Teacher Yasmin ask the class to remember before the play?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They have practised hard, they must be gentle and polite backstage, and they should smile and keep going after a mistake.
comprehension.explanation: The talk is organised with First, Second and Third, so each point can be listed in order.

comprehension.question: Why does Nora say she feels curious?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Nora is curious because she is visiting a cultural fair tomorrow and has never tried food from so many places.
comprehension.explanation: She gives her reason in the same turn, using the present continuous for the arranged plan.

comprehension.question: Which part did Amal play in the school play, and why did it matter to her?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She played the kind queen who helps people in need, and it was her first ever school play.
comprehension.explanation: The narrator gives both the role and the fact that Amal had never acted before, which raises the pressure.

comprehension.question: What did Adam tell Amal about his own experience of tests?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Adam said he had felt nervous before a test too, and that it was fine.
comprehension.explanation: Adam shares a life experience in the present perfect so that his sister feels less alone.

comprehension.question: What does Nora mean when she says her friends come from many ethnic groups?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She means their families come from different cultures and home places, from the city to farming villages and other countries.
comprehension.explanation: The sentence straight after the word ethnic lists the different backgrounds, which shows the meaning in context.

comprehension.question: Teacher Yasmin says not to be selfish with the costumes. What kind of sentence is that, and what does it ask for?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It is a negative imperative, and it asks everybody to share the costumes fairly backstage.
comprehension.explanation: Sentences that begin with Don't give direct advice, so the class hears exactly what behaviour is expected.

comprehension.question: What made Maya feel proud when she went to the fair last year?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Maya felt proud because she showed her family's food to everybody at the fair.
comprehension.explanation: Maya answers her own experience question, which is the detail that explains her pride.

comprehension.question: Why does Amal decide it would be selfish to leave the new student on her own?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The new student looked terrified and stood alone, so walking away would put Amal's comfort first.
comprehension.explanation: Amal has just learned how frightening it feels to stand in front of strangers, so she chooses kindness over comfort.

comprehension.question: Mum tells Amal to be polite to her worry. What is Mum really asking her to do?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She is asking Amal to notice the worry calmly and then let it settle, instead of fighting it.
comprehension.explanation: The joke works because you cannot argue a worry away, but you can treat it gently and put it to sleep.

comprehension.question: Nora's grandmother says a guest is a gift. Which detail shows the family lives by that saying?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Her grandmother bakes sweet honey cakes for the guests, which is a generous welcome.
comprehension.explanation: Baking for visitors is the evidence in the text that turns the saying into an action.

grammar.title: Present Perfect (for life experiences)
grammar.explanation: We use the present perfect for things we have done or felt at some time in our life, when the exact time does not matter. It links the past to now, so “I have felt nervous before” tells your listener that the feeling is part of who you are today.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use this pattern: subject + have / has + past participle.
Use have with I, you, we and they: “I have travelled to many places.”
Use has with he, she and it: “She has never been shy.”
The past participle is the third form of the verb. Regular verbs add -ed (play → played), and irregular verbs change shape (go → gone, eat → eaten, be → been).
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often write “I have eat lunch.” The present perfect needs the past participle, not the base verb, so write “I have eaten lunch.” The second slip is “She have seen that film”; he, she and it always take has, giving “She has seen that film.”
grammar.memoryTip: Picture have and has as a bridge from your past to right now. He, she and it always cross that bridge with has.
grammar.practice: Complete each sentence in the present perfect, then check yourself against the answers. | 1. I __________ (never / try) mango juice. | 2. He __________ (see) that film three times. | 3. They __________ (travel) to Kenya. | 4. She __________ (not / be) to a concert. | Answers: 1. have never tried 2. has seen 3. have travelled 4. has not (hasn’t) been.

grammar.title: Present Continuous for Future Plans
grammar.explanation: The present continuous is not only for actions happening this minute. We also use it for future plans that are already arranged, so it tells people what we have decided to do later.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use this pattern: subject + am / is / are + verb-ing + a future time word.
Use am with I, is with he, she and it, and are with you, we and they.
Add a future time word such as tomorrow, next week or on Friday.
Example: “We are visiting a cultural fair tomorrow.”
grammar.commonMistake: A frequent slip is “I am go to the fair tomorrow.” The main verb needs -ing, giving “I am going to the fair tomorrow.” Dropping the time word is the other slip, because without tomorrow your listener thinks you mean this very moment.
grammar.memoryTip: Treat this future as a promise already written in your diary. Say the time word out loud and nobody will think you mean now.
grammar.practice: Put each verb into the present continuous for a future plan. | 1. I __________ (visit) my grandparents this weekend. | 2. They __________ (have) a picnic next Sunday. | 3. She __________ (join) the football team next month. | 4. We __________ (watch) a film tonight. | Answers: 1. am visiting 2. are having 3. is joining 4. are watching.

grammar.title: Past Simple (for finished actions)
grammar.explanation: The past simple describes actions that started and finished in the past. It is the tense that carries a story along, as in “She felt anxious last night.”
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Regular verbs add -ed: play → played, walk → walked.
Irregular verbs change in their own way: go → went, see → saw, eat → ate, feel → felt.
Add a past time word such as yesterday, last night or last week.
Example: “Amal studied her spelling words every evening.”
grammar.commonMistake: “She feels anxious last night” puts two different times in one sentence. Move the verb back: “She felt anxious last night.” Irregular verbs need care too, because “She feeled” is never correct.
grammar.memoryTip: Regular verbs put on an -ed coat for yesterday. Irregular verbs each wear their own costume, so learn two or three of them every day.
grammar.practice: Write the past simple form of each verb in brackets. | 1. I __________ (play) football after school yesterday. | 2. They __________ (go) to the zoo last weekend. | 3. She __________ (feel) tired after the party. | 4. He __________ (eat) rice for dinner yesterday. | Answers: 1. played 2. went 3. felt 4. ate.

practiceAudio.status: Refused - the script is a fill-in-the-blank frame; needs a spoken form

grammar.title: Imperatives for Advice and Safety
grammar.explanation: Imperatives are sentences that give advice, instructions or safety tips. They tell people clearly what to do, or what not to do, so that everybody stays safe and kind.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Start with the base form of the verb: “Be polite.” “Listen to your teacher.”
For negative advice, start with Don’t: “Don’t be selfish.”
You never need the word you, because it is already understood.
Add Always or Please to sound friendly: “Always say thank you.”
grammar.commonMistake: Many learners write “You be polite.” Drop the pronoun and simply say “Be polite.” The second slip is adding -ly to the describing word, as in “Don’t be selfishly”; keep the plain adjective and write “Don’t be selfish.”
grammar.memoryTip: An imperative is a friendly nudge, not a shout. Begin with the bare verb and the sentence is already complete.
grammar.practice: Write the correct imperative in each gap, then read your answers aloud. | 1. __________ (be) careful when you cross the road. | 2. __________ (not / touch) the hot stove! | 3. __________ (always / say) thank you. | 4. __________ (not / interrupt) when somebody is speaking. | Answers: 1. Be 2. Don’t touch 3. Always say 4. Don’t interrupt.

grammar.title: Modal Verbs for Advice (must, mustn't, should)
grammar.explanation: Modal verbs such as must, mustn’t and should are helping verbs that carry advice. They let us separate what is truly necessary from what is simply a good idea.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use this pattern: subject + modal verb + base form of the verb.
must = strong advice that really matters: “You must wash your hands before eating.”
mustn’t = do not do this at all: “You mustn’t run in the corridor.”
should = softer advice, a good idea: “You should be gentle with others.”
grammar.commonMistake: “You must goes outside” adds an ending that modal verbs never allow, so write “You must go outside.” Choosing must for gentle advice also sounds harsh; when you are only suggesting, use should, as in “You should relax.”
grammar.memoryTip: must is a firm hand on your shoulder, mustn’t is a red traffic light, and should is a friendly suggestion from a friend.
grammar.practice: Choose must, mustn’t or should for each sentence. | 1. You __________ eat your vegetables to stay healthy. | 2. You __________ leave your toys on the floor; pick them up! | 3. You __________ say kind things to your friends. | 4. You __________ talk to strangers you do not know. | Answers: 1. must 2. mustn’t 3. should 4. mustn’t.

grammar.title: Question Forms + Descriptive Collocations
grammar.explanation: This lesson joins two skills that work together. A good question opens a conversation, and natural word pairs, called collocations, make the answers sound like real English.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Yes / No questions begin with a verb: “Do you like football?” “Are you happy?”
Wh- questions begin with a question word such as who, what, where, when, why or how: “How do you feel today?”
For life experiences, use the present perfect: “Have you ever felt proud?”
Every question ends with a question mark.
Collocations pair one adjective with the noun it suits best: anxious thoughts, fierce debate, proud smile, gentle voice.
grammar.commonMistake: Writing “You are happy?” keeps statement order, so swap the first two words and write “Are you happy?” Forgetting the mark after “How do you feel today” is the next slip. With collocations, “fierce thoughts” sounds strange to an English ear; choose the partner that fits and write “anxious thoughts.”
grammar.memoryTip: Every question word is a key that unlocks new information, so turn the key first and add the mark last. For collocations, trust your ear: if two words sound like a team, keep them together.
grammar.practice: Part A: turn each statement into a question. | 1. You like football. → __________? | 2. She is happy. → __________? | 3. They went to the park. → __________? | Part B: choose the word that makes the natural collocation. | 4. I had __________ (anxious / happy) thoughts before the exam. | 5. The class had one __________ (fierce / soft) debate about the best game. | 6. She gave me one __________ (sad / proud) smile after my presentation. | Answers: 1. Do you like football? 2. Is she happy? 3. Did they go to the park? 4. anxious 5. fierce 6. proud.

writing.title: Writing 1: A Feelings Blog Post
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a blog post of four or five sentences called “A Day I Felt ______”.
Choose one feeling, such as anxious, curious or proud.
Tell what happened, how you felt, and what you did next.
Use the past simple for the events, and add one present perfect sentence.
writing.modelText: A Day I Felt Curious. Last Saturday I found an old wooden box under the stairs. I felt curious, so I asked Mum what was inside it. She showed me photographs of her first school. I have felt curious about our family ever since that afternoon.
writing.successCriteria: I chose one clear feeling; I told the events in the past simple; I included one present perfect sentence; I checked every capital letter and full stop.
writing.support: Say the whole post aloud before you write it, and keep your Word Wall open beside you.
writing.extension: Add two sentences explaining what you would tell a friend who felt the same way.

writing.title: Writing 2: A Mini-Guide: How to Be Kind at School
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a short guide titled “How to Be Polite and Kind at School”.
Give five pieces of advice, using imperatives and modal verbs.
Number each piece so your reader can follow the guide easily.
Finish with one sentence saying why kindness matters in your class.
writing.modelText:
How to Be Polite and Kind at School.
1. Always say please and thank you.
2. You should share your equipment, and never be selfish.
3. Don’t be rough; be gentle with younger children.
4. Listen politely when somebody else is speaking.
5. You must tell an adult if a classmate is upset.
Kindness makes our classroom safe for every single person.
writing.expectedLength: 5 numbered tips plus one closing sentence
writing.successCriteria: I wrote five numbered tips; I used at least two imperatives and two modal verbs; my closing sentence gives a reason; my spelling of the unit words is correct.
writing.support: Look back at Grammar 4 and Grammar 5 for the sentence patterns before you begin.
writing.extension: Turn your five tips into a poster with one drawing for each piece of advice.

writing.title: Writing 3: Proud of My Identity
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write three or four sentences about your family background, or about one tradition you are proud of.
You could write about a special food, a language you speak at home, or a celebration such as harvest or a birthday.
Use the word ethnic once, and make its meaning clear from your sentence.
Read your writing aloud to check that it still sounds like you.
writing.modelText: My family comes from two different ethnic backgrounds, so we bake two kinds of bread. At home we speak one language with my grandmother and English at school. Every harvest we gather in the garden and share honey cakes with our neighbours. I am proud that our table always has room for one more chair.
writing.successCriteria: I named one real tradition; I used ethnic accurately; I gave one detail a reader could picture; I ended with how the tradition makes me feel.
writing.support: Talk to somebody at home first and note three words you want to use.
writing.extension: Interview an older relative and add one sentence quoting exactly what they said.

writing.title: Writing 4: Connected Paragraph
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write one paragraph of six sentences about a time you helped somebody who felt shy.
Join your ideas with connectives such as because, although, so and after that.
Keep every sentence in the same tense, and check each full stop.
Underline the two connectives you think work best.
writing.modelText: Our new classmate stood alone by the wall because she did not know anybody. I felt nervous too, although I really wanted to help her. I asked her to sit with us, so she carried her lunch across the yard. After that, Maya taught her the words of our clapping game. She smiled at last, and she has joined us every break time since. Being generous with your time costs nothing at all.
writing.successCriteria: My paragraph holds one clear story; I used at least three different connectives; my tense stays the same throughout; I underlined my two best connectives.
writing.support: Write your six ideas as short notes first, then join them into sentences.
writing.extension: Rewrite the paragraph from the shy classmate's point of view.

writing.title: Writing 5: Information Text
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a short information text called “Feelings Are Signals” for younger readers.
Use one main heading and two sections, each with its own subheading.
Explain two feelings words, then give one practical tip for each feeling.
Set your tips out as bullet points so the page is easy to read.
writing.modelText:
Feelings Are Signals.
When You Feel Nervous: Nervous means worried about something that has not happened yet.
• Breathe out slowly five times.
• Tell one adult what is worrying you.
When You Feel Terrified: Terrified means very frightened indeed.
• Move to somewhere safe and bright.
• Say out loud what frightened you.
writing.successCriteria: My headings match my sections; each feeling has a clear meaning; each tip is one short instruction; my layout helps a younger reader.
writing.support: Copy the layout of the model text first, then swap in your own two feelings.
writing.extension: Add a third section about a feeling that is pleasant, such as proud or curious.

writing.title: Writing 6: Reflect and Improve
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Read your Writing 1 blog post again, two days after you wrote it.
Mark one sentence you like and one sentence that could be clearer.
Rewrite the weaker sentence twice, choosing a stronger feelings word each time.
Then write two sentences explaining what you improved and why it helps your reader.
writing.modelText: My best sentence was “My hands shook while I waited for my turn.” My weakest sentence was “I was sad.” Better version one: “I felt doubtful that I could remember my lines.” Better version two: “I felt anxious, and my thoughts would not stay still.” I improved my writing by choosing exact feelings words instead of easy ones. Precise words let my reader picture the moment clearly.
writing.successCriteria: I marked one strong and one weak sentence; I rewrote the weak one twice; each rewrite uses a precise feelings word; my reflection names the improvement.
writing.support: Use the Word Wall to find a sharper word before you rewrite.
writing.extension: Swap posts with a partner and suggest one improvement to their weakest sentence.

activities.title: Activities 1: Match the Feeling
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Match each feeling word to what that person might say, then write the four pairs.
1. terrified — a) “I really want to know what is inside that box!”
2. curious — b) “There is a huge spider on the wall!”
3. proud — c) “I worked so hard, and I finished it all by myself.”
4. shy — d) “I don’t want to speak in front of everyone.”
activities.answerSummary: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d. The spider shows fear, the box shows wanting to know, the finished job shows pride, and not wanting to speak shows shyness.

activities.title: Activities 2: Behaviour: Kind or Unkind?
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write kind or unkind beside each action, then name the unit word that fits it.
1. Sharing your snack with a friend who has none.
2. Taking all the toys and not letting others play.
3. Speaking gently to a new student.
4. Laughing at somebody who has made a mistake.
activities.answerSummary: 1. kind, generous. 2. unkind, selfish. 3. kind, gentle and polite. 4. unkind. Item 4 has no single unit word, so accept any reasoned answer.

activities.title: Activities 3: Fill in the Feeling
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Complete each sentence with one feelings word from this unit.
1. Before the big test, I felt ______.
2. When I saw the huge dog, I was ______.
3. I finished my project all by myself, so I felt ______.
4. The new girl was too ______ to talk to anybody.
activities.answerSummary: 1. nervous or anxious. 2. terrified. 3. proud. 4. shy. Doubtful works in item 1 only if the learner explains the doubt.

activities.instructionsAndItems:
Hunt for evidence in the story “The Day of the Play”.

quizzes.question: Which word means feeling worried or a little afraid about something that might happen?
quizzes.explanation: Nervous names that worried feeling. Attract is an action, a dishwasher is a machine, and frequent describes how often something happens.

quizzes.question: Amal shook and could not sit still before her spelling test. Which word describes her best?
quizzes.explanation: Anxious describes a very worried feeling. Generous, humorous and polite all describe how a person behaves towards others.

quizzes.question: What does the word generous mean?
quizzes.options: Happy to share or give to others | Very bad or cruel | Happening often, or many times | Quiet and afraid to talk to people
quizzes.correctAnswer: Happy to share or give to others
quizzes.explanation: The other three options are the meanings of evil, frequent and shy.

quizzes.question: Which sentence shows selfish behaviour?
quizzes.options: Sami gave half of his sandwich away. | Maya held the classroom door open for her teacher. | Amal listened while the new girl spoke. | A child kept every paintbrush and shared none.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A child kept every paintbrush and shared none.
quizzes.explanation: Keeping everything for yourself is selfish. The other three sentences show generous, polite and gentle behaviour.

quizzes.question: Complete this life-experience sentence: “I ______ never tried mango juice.”
quizzes.explanation: The subject is I, so the present perfect uses have with the past participle tried.
quizzes.origin: Generated from this unit's reading passages

quizzes.question: Which sentence describes a plan that is already arranged for tomorrow?
quizzes.options: We visited the fair yesterday. | We are visiting the fair tomorrow. | We visit the fair every single year. | We have visited the fair twice.
quizzes.correctAnswer: We are visiting the fair tomorrow.
quizzes.explanation: The present continuous plus a future time word signals an arranged plan, not a habit or a finished action.
quizzes.origin: Generated from this unit's reading passages

quizzes.question: Complete this past simple sentence: “She ______ tired after the long party.”
quizzes.explanation: Feel is irregular, so its past simple form is felt rather than feeled.
quizzes.origin: Generated from this unit's reading passages

quizzes.question: Which sentence gives advice using a modal verb?
quizzes.options: Don’t run in the hall. | You should be gentle with the puppy. | Are you feeling shy today? | The wind was fierce last night.
quizzes.correctAnswer: You should be gentle with the puppy.
quizzes.explanation: Should is the modal verb. The first option is an imperative, the third is a question, and the fourth is past simple.

quizzes.question: Which question about a life experience is written correctly?
quizzes.options: You have ever felt proud? | Have you ever proud felt? | Did you ever have felt proud? | Have you ever felt proud?
quizzes.explanation: A present perfect question puts have before the subject, then ever, then the past participle felt.
quizzes.origin: Generated from this unit's reading passages

quizzes.question: The class argued strongly about the best game. Which phrase describes that talk naturally?
quizzes.options: a fierce debate | a gentle debate | a shy debate | a curious debate
quizzes.explanation: Fierce and debate are a natural collocation. Gentle, shy and curious do not partner debate in everyday English.

teacherNotes.note: Pre-teach the six Group 1 feelings words with facial expressions before Reading 1, because doubtful and terrified will be new for many learners. Keep the emotional talk light: invite volunteers and never require a child to share a private worry. Accept single words from quieter learners during Feelings Charades, then model the full sentence back to them. Mark the present perfect for meaning first and for form second.

An adult stays beside the learner for every AI-tutor task in this unit, and no child works alone with the device. Suggested prompts by section. Vocabulary: “Can you quiz me on the feelings words and tell me the difference between nervous and anxious?” Reading: “Can you read The Day Before the Test with me and explain any hard words?” Grammar: “Why do we say I have felt rather than I felt for a life experience?” Speaking: “Can you play Feelings Charades and guess the word I act out?” Writing: “Can you check my blog post and tell me one thing to fix?” Remind learners that the tutor prepares them for the teacher session; it does not replace it.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d. Award one mark per pair. If a learner links proud to the spider line, ask which words in b) show fear.
1 kind (generous), 2 unkind (selfish), 3 kind (gentle and polite), 4 unkind. Full marks need the unit word as well as the kind or unkind label.
1 nervous or anxious, 2 terrified, 3 proud, 4 shy. Accept doubtful for item 1 only when the learner adds a sentence explaining the doubt.
1 nervously, 2 politely, 3 gently, 4 frequently, 5 seriously. Item 3 carries the teaching point, because gentle drops its final e before -ly.
Feelings: doubtful, curious. Behaviour: generous, humorous, selfish, evil. Identity and everyday life: ethnic, dishwasher, risky, attract. The sentence about evil carries two of the five marks.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: 1 “I’m so nervous,” she whispered. 2 “But you’ve done harder things.” 3 “You were very gentle on the stage,” the girl said at last. 4 nervous, risky, gentle. Quotations must be copied exactly, including the speech marks.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: nervous. The learner matches a definition to a feelings word; attract, dishwasher and frequent belong to other word classes.
anxious. Shaking and being unable to sit still are the physical signs of the strong worry that anxious names.
Happy to share or give to others. The three wrong options are the meanings of evil, frequent and shy.
A child kept every paintbrush and shared none. Keeping everything for yourself defines selfish; the others show generous, polite and gentle behaviour.
have. The subject I takes have, and the present perfect then needs the past participle tried.
We are visiting the fair tomorrow. Present continuous plus a future time word marks an arranged plan rather than a habit.
felt. Feel is irregular, so learners who write feeled need the irregular verb list again.
You should be gentle with the puppy. Should is the modal; the distractors are an imperative, a question and a past simple statement.
Have you ever felt proud? Present perfect questions invert have and the subject, then add ever and the past participle.
a fierce debate. Fierce partners debate naturally; gentle, shy and curious do not, which is the collocation point from Grammar 6.
